claim: 114 genes on chromosome 17q are essential to neuroblastoma cell survival.
source: Analysis of the cancer dependency genes in neuroblastoma cell lines screened with the Avana sgRNA library (Meyers et al., 2017) revealed that 114 were essential to neuroblastoma (mean score <−0.4) (Figure 1A, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by CRISPR screening data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Proteins encoded by 114 essential genes on 17q form distinct but interconnected modules including RNA splicing, mitochondrial metabolism, protein homeostasis, DNA repair, transcriptional regulation, and endocytosis.
source: Protein interaction network analysis followed by functional annotation revealed that proteins encoded by these 114 essential genes formed distinct but interconnected modules including RNA splicing (i.e. SRSF2, DDX5, DDX42, DHX8), mitochondrial metabolism (i.e. NDUFA8, COX11, SLC25A10, SLC35B1), protein homeostasis (i.e. UBE2O, PSMB3, PSMC5), DNA repair (i.e. BRIP1, BRCA1, RAD51C, RAD51D) and transcriptional regulation (i.e. PHF12, CBX1, SMARCE1, MED1), as well as endocytosis (i.e. CHMP6, CTLC, EPN3, HGS, SNF8, VPS25) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by protein interaction network analysis shown in Figure 1B

claim: 81 of the 114 essential genes on 17q were highly expressed in high-risk neuroblastomas.
source: Using these 114 genes as a signature, we found that 81 of them were highly expressed in high-risk neuroblastomas, which were enriched with MYCN amplification (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1C

claim: High-risk neuroblastomas are enriched with MYCN amplification.
source: Using these 114 genes as a signature, we found that 81 of them were highly expressed in high-risk neuroblastomas, which were enriched with MYCN amplification (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Neuroblastomas with high expression levels of the 114 essential gene signature were associated with poorer event-free and overall survival of patients.
source: Correspondingly, neuroblastomas with high expression levels of this gene signature were associated with a poorer event-free (time from treatment until the cancer progresses) and overall survival (time from treatment to death) of patients in two large clinic cohorts (Figure 1D and E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figures 1D and 1E

claim: In low-risk neuroblastoma patients, high expression of the 114 essential genes was associated with poor event-free and overall survival.
source: Interestingly, in low-risk neuroblastoma patients, high expression of the 114 essential genes was associated with poor event-free and overall survival, while no difference was observed in high-risk patients (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: In high-risk neuroblastoma patients, expression of the 114 essential genes showed no difference in event-free and overall survival.
source: Interestingly, in low-risk neuroblastoma patients, high expression of the 114 essential genes was associated with poor event-free and overall survival, while no difference was observed in high-risk patients (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: The 114 essential genes cannot further stratify the high-risk patients.

claim: Among the genes encoding JmjC domain containing proteins, JMJD6 was the only one that was frequently amplified in neuroblastoma.

claim: High JMJD6 expression was associated with poor event-free outcome.
source: High JMJD6 expression was associated with poor event-free outcome, as shown by Kaplan-Meier analysis (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 2B

claim: High levels of JMJD6 expression was associated with poor event-free and overall survival in both low-risk and high-risk patients.
source: Further analysis of JMJD6 expression in low-risk and high-risk patients showed that high levels of JMJD6 expression was associated with poor event-free and overall survival in both low-risk and high-risk patients (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that JMJD6 is high-risk factor regardless of disease status.

claim: JMJD6 is a high-risk factor regardless of disease status.

evidence: Inferred from the association of JMJD6 with poor survival in both low-risk and high-risk patients

claim: JMJD6 was amplified across multiple types of adult cancers such as breast and liver cancer.

evidence: Supported by genomic data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A

claim: JMJD6 amplification correlated with worse relapse-free survival in adult cancers.
source: JMJD6 was amplified across multiple types of adult cancers such as breast and liver cancer (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), and correlated with worse relapse-free survival (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B

claim: JMJD6 showed the highest expression levels in neuroblastoma compared to over 20 pediatric cancer subtypes.
source: We further compared the RNA-seq expression of JMJD6 in 2337 samples across over 20 pediatric cancer subtypes and found that JMJD6 showed the highest expression levels in neuroblastoma (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), suggesting that JMJD6 might be particularly important in neuroblastoma.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C

claim: JMJD6 might be particularly important in neuroblastoma.

evidence: Inferred from the highest expression of JMJD6 in neuroblastoma

claim: Loss of JMJD6 greatly reduced the colony numbers in all tested neuroblastoma cell lines.

The results showed that loss of JMJD6 greatly reduced the colony numbers in all tested cell lines (Figure 2C and Materials and methods), demonstrating that JMJD6 is essential to neuroblastoma cells regardless of MYCN amplification.
evidence: Supported by colony formation assay shown in Figure 2C

claim: JMJD6 is essential to neuroblastoma cells regardless of MYCN amplification.

The results showed that loss of JMJD6 greatly reduced the colony numbers in all tested cell lines (Figure 2C and Materials and methods), demonstrating that JMJD6 is essential to neuroblastoma cells regardless of MYCN amplification.
evidence: Inferred from the effect of JMJD6 knockdown in both MYCN-amplified and non-amplified cells

claim: The extent of differentiation in neuroblastoma tumor cells is correlated with prognostic significance.

claim: Loss of JMJD6 led to neurite outgrowth.

evidence: Based on established knowledge of neuroblastoma cell differentiation

claim: JMJD6 is required to regulate cellular differentiation.

claim: Overexpression of MYCN induced foci formation with enhanced cell death in NIH3T3 cells.

claim: JMJD6 enhances MYCN activity to transform NIH3T3 cells.
